detailedExplanation: This topic is verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Biology Curriculum Outline 2026–27 and the corresponding AQA GCSE Biology 8461 content.

Cells in a multicellular organism do not all perform the same job. During development, cells become specialised. This process is called differentiation. As a cell differentiates, it develops particular structures that allow it to carry out a particular function.

Examples in animals include sperm cells, nerve cells and muscle cells. A sperm cell has a tail for movement and many mitochondria to transfer energy needed for swimming. A nerve cell has a long axon so electrical impulses can travel over long distances. Muscle cells contain many mitochondria because contraction requires a large transfer of energy.

Examples in plants include root hair cells, xylem cells and phloem cells. Root hair cells have a long extension that increases surface area for absorption of water and mineral ions. Xylem cells form hollow tubes and are strengthened to transport water and support the plant. Phloem transports dissolved sugars around the plant.

Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage and later lose much of their ability to change into other cell types. Many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate throughout the life of the plant.
You must explain how specialised cells are adapted to their functions and understand how differentiation produces specialised cells.
